title: Nehemiah 5:14–19
context: Nehemiah describes his own conduct as governor for twelve years, from Artaxerxes' twentieth to thirty-second year. Unlike earlier governors, he did not take the governor's food allowance or burden the people, "because of the fear of God." He kept working on the wall, bought no land, and fed a large table at his own expense. He closes with a prayer: "Remember me, my God, for all the good that I have done for this people."

verses.text: Moreover from the time that I was appointed to be their governor in the land of Judah, from the twentieth year even to the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes the king, that is, twelve years, I and my brothers have not eaten the bread of the governor.
verses.arminianNotes: From the twentieth to the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes, Nehemiah and his brothers have not eaten "the bread of the governor." Arminian readers note his deliberate choice to give up a right for the people's sake.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the twelve years span from Nehemiah 2:1 to 13:6. Paul similarly gave up his rights so as to "cause no hindrance to the Good News of Christ" (1 Corinthians 9:12).

verses.text: But the former governors who were before me were supported by the people, and took bread and wine from them, plus forty shekels of silver; yes, even their servants ruled over the people, but I didn’t do so, because of the fear of God.
verses.arminianNotes: The former governors burdened the people, “but I didn’t do so, because of the fear of God.” Arminian readers see a leader whose reverence for God shapes how he uses his power.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the fear of God is again the motive, as in verse 9. Peter later calls leaders to serve "not as lording it over those entrusted to you" (1 Peter 5:3).

verses.text: Yes, I also continued in the work of this wall. We didn’t buy any land. All my servants were gathered there to the work.
verses.arminianNotes: Nehemiah continued in the work, bought no land, and set his servants to the work. Arminian readers note that he avoided profiting from the crisis, keeping his focus on the task God gave him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that a governor could have acquired land cheaply during the famine. Nehemiah's refusal shows integrity that matches the reform he demanded of the nobles.

verses.text: Moreover there were at my table, of the Jews and the rulers, one hundred fifty men, in addition to those who came to us from among the nations that were around us.
verses.arminianNotes: A hundred fifty Jews and rulers ate at his table, plus visitors from the nations. Arminian readers see generous hospitality offered at personal cost to strengthen the community.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the governor's table was a public responsibility. Nehemiah carries it himself rather than passing the cost on to a struggling people.

verses.text: Now that which was prepared for one day was one ox and six choice sheep. Also fowls were prepared for me, and once in ten days a store of all sorts of wine. Yet for all this, I didn’t demand the governor’s pay, because the bondage was heavy on this people.
verses.arminianNotes: Each day an ox, six sheep, and fowls were prepared, yet he did not demand the governor's pay "because the bondage was heavy on this people." Arminian readers note his compassion for those already burdened.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Nehemiah's generosity flows from attention to the people's condition. Paul likewise worked "that we might not burden any of you" (2 Thessalonians 3:8).

verses.text: Remember me, my God, for all the good that I have done for this people.
verses.arminianNotes: "Remember me, my God, for all the good that I have done for this people." Arminian readers see a servant's honest appeal to God, trusting that faithful service is noticed and valued by him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this kind of prayer recurs in Nehemiah 13:14, 22, and 31. In 13:22 he also asks God to “spare me according to the greatness of your loving kindness.” His hope rests on God’s kindness.
